title: Common Grace
subtitle: What Pastors Learn When They Listen to the World
blurb: God did not lock his goodness inside the church. He scattered it across the whole field of human life — into the laboratory, the studio, the courtroom, the mouth of the honest unbeliever — and called it good before any of us got there. This is a book about the grace that is common: the kindness of God to those who do not yet know his name, and the discipline of learning to recognize it without surrendering to it.

chapters.title: The Field Was Already His
chapters.summary: Common grace is not a concession to secularism but a doctrine with deep Reformed roots — God's restraining and gifting goodness toward all people, believer and unbeliever alike. The pastor who denies it ends up smaller than the God he claims to serve.
chapters.body:
I spent the first part of my life certain that the church had nothing I needed. I was not angry at God. You cannot be angry at someone you are sure does not exist. I was simply convinced that the interesting people, the honest people, the ones asking real questions, were all standing outside the building. And when I finally walked in, I expected to find that the people inside believed the same thing in reverse — that everything outside was darkness, and the only light was in here.

Some of them did believe that. They still do.

This is the first thing I want to say, and I want to say it slowly. The instinct to draw a hard line between the holy church and the godless world is older than any of us, and it feels like faithfulness. It feels like guarding something. But it is not faithfulness. It is a failure of nerve dressed up as purity, and it makes God smaller than the Bible says he is.

Consider the sentence Jesus drops into the Sermon on the Mount almost in passing. He tells us to love our enemies, and he gives the reason: God "makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust" (Matthew 5:45). Read that again. The sun and the rain — the two things that make any harvest possible, the difference between a family eating and a family starving — God gives them to people who curse him. He does not means-test his kindness. The atheist's wheat grows. The blasphemer's children are healthy. The cruel man's orchard bears fruit.

The Reformed tradition gave this a name. Common grace. Not saving grace — that is a different thing, the grace that rescues and regenerates and brings a dead heart to life. Common grace is the goodness of God that falls on the whole human race without distinction: the grace that restrains evil, that gives gifts of intellect and art and craft and governance, that keeps the world from collapsing into the chaos our sin deserves. John Calvin, who is too often caricatured as a man who saw only depravity, wrote in the Institutes that we must not despise the truth wherever it appears, because to do so would be to insult the Spirit of God who is its source. He was clear that the Spirit who saves is also the Spirit who gives the pagan astronomer his eyes and the pagan jurist his sense of justice.

Calvin meant it. He read the Roman lawyers. He admired the Greek philosophers. He could not bring himself to consign their genius to the devil, because he knew where genius comes from.

We have lost this. Somewhere along the way large parts of the American church decided that to honor God we had to dishonor everything God made outside the sanctuary. We built a parallel universe — our own music, our own movies, our own bookstores, our own celebrities — and we told ourselves it was holiness. It was not holiness. It was fear with a Bible verse taped to it. And the cost has been enormous, because a church that cannot recognize God's fingerprints in a Beethoven symphony or a vaccine or a just law will eventually fail to recognize them anywhere at all.

I am implicating myself here. For years I preached as though the only true things in the world were the things said from a pulpit. I treated the doctor's diagnosis as less real than the prayer offered over the patient, when in fact both were gifts of the same hand. I was not being faithful. I was being provincial, and I called it conviction.

Abraham Kuyper, the Dutch theologian who became prime minister of the Netherlands in 1901, said the thing that has never let me go. There is not one square inch of the whole domain of human existence over which Christ, who is sovereign over all, does not cry out, "Mine." Hear what that actually claims. Not that the church owns every square inch. That Christ does. The laboratory is his. The concert hall is his. The secular university, the city council, the Tuesday afternoon shift at the factory — his, all of it, whether the people working there know it or not.

Which means the pastor's task is not to defend a shrinking territory. It is to go out into a world that already belongs to his Lord and learn to recognize the Owner's handiwork in places the Owner's people forgot to look.

The Psalmist understood this long before Calvin or Kuyper. "The earth is the LORD's and the fullness thereof, the world and those who dwell therein" (Psalm 24:1). The fullness. Not the church and the rest is up for grabs. The fullness. And in the next breath the same tradition tells us that the heavens declare the glory of God and the sky proclaims his handiwork, that day to day pours out speech (Psalm 19:1-2) — a speech going out into all the earth, to people who have never opened a Bible. God has been preaching to the whole world through the world itself since before the first sermon was ever written.

Here is what this does to a pastor who takes it seriously. It ends the war. Not the war against sin — that war is real and we will speak of it. The other war, the manufactured one, the one we wage against human culture as though culture itself were the enemy. That war was never ours to fight. God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world but that the world might be saved through him (John 3:17), and a church that spends its energy condemning the world has misread the direction its own Savior was traveling.

I am not asking you to baptize everything. We will spend much of this book learning to test, to discern, to refuse. There is real darkness, and naming it is part of the calling. But you cannot test what you refuse to listen to. You cannot discern in a culture you have walled yourself off from. And you cannot love your neighbor while believing that everything your neighbor has made, thought, built, and loved is worthless.

When I came in from the outside, the people who reached me were not the ones who told me my whole world was a lie. They were the ones who said: that hunger you have for truth, that ache for justice, that thing in you that cannot stand a cheap answer — that is not from nowhere. That is the image of God in you, and you have been listening to him longer than you know.

They were right. I had been. So have your skeptics. So has your city.

The field was already his. We are only late to the harvest.
chapters.verdict: The world is not God's enemy. It is God's field, and he was working it before we arrived.
reflect: Where have you treated a gift of God as a threat simply because it came from outside the church?
What would change in your preaching if you believed God was already speaking to your skeptics before you opened your mouth?
Name one good thing in your city you have never once thanked God for.

chapters.title: All Truth Is God's Truth
chapters.summary: The ancient principle that truth belongs to God wherever it is found frees the pastor to learn from anyone without fear — and obligates him to test everything against Scripture rather than against his own comfort.
chapters.body:
Augustine put it plainly sixteen centuries ago, and the church has been forgetting it ever since. He told the Christians of his day that if the pagan philosophers had said anything true, anything just, we should not shrink from it but should claim it for our own use — the way Israel carried the gold of Egypt out into the wilderness. The gold was good gold. It did not become idolatrous because Egyptians had mined it. The sin of Egypt was in the calf they made; the gold itself was God's, and God's people were right to carry it out.

All truth is God's truth. The phrase is not in the Bible, but the conviction runs through it like a seam of ore. The line gets attributed to several teachers across the centuries, and the exact wording matters less than the claim underneath it. If something is true, it is true because it corresponds to the way God made reality. There is no truth that God does not author, because there is no reality he did not make. So when a true thing is spoken, it does not matter whether it comes from a prophet or a physicist or an atheist who would laugh you out of the room for praying. The truth is on loan to them from God, and you may receive it without apology.

I know how dangerous that sounds to careful people. They hear "all truth is God's truth" and they think it is a door propped open for every error to walk through. So let me close the door I am not opening. The principle does not say that everything anyone claims is true. It does not say that the spirit of the age should set the agenda for the church. It says something much narrower and much harder: that when something is in fact true, its source does not disqualify it, and our refusal to receive it is not piety but pride.

The hard part is the testing. Because the same world that gives us true things also gives us counterfeit things, and the two come mixed. The Apostle Paul, writing to a church surrounded by Greek philosophy and Roman power, did not tell them to plug their ears. He told them: "test everything; hold fast what is good" (1 Thessalonians 5:21). Test everything. That is not the instruction of a man afraid of ideas. It is the instruction of a man confident that truth can survive examination and that error will not.

But notice the standard of the test. Paul does not say test everything against your preferences. He does not say test everything against what the congregation will tolerate. The standard is the revealed word of God. The Bereans were called noble precisely because, when even Paul preached to them, they searched the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so (Acts 17:11). They tested the apostle. They were commended for it. The measure is always Scripture, never our comfort, and the difference between those two things is where most of us go wrong.

Here is the trap, and I have fallen into it. We tell ourselves we are testing an idea against the Bible when we are actually testing it against our culture, our politics, our upbringing, the assumptions of the people we eat lunch with. We reject a true thing because it offends our tribe, and we congratulate ourselves on our faithfulness. We accept a false thing because our tribe approves of it, and we never run it past the text at all. The discipline of common grace is not the discipline of saying yes to the world. It is the discipline of saying yes only to what is true and no only to what is false, by the one standard that is not ours to bend.

Consider science, since it is the place this fight gets loudest. When a researcher discovers how a cell repairs its own DNA, that researcher has read a sentence God wrote into the structure of life. The discovery is true whether the researcher believes in God or not. Kepler, who worked out the laws of planetary motion in the early seventeenth century, said he was thinking God's thoughts after him. He was a man of faith, but the thing he discovered would have been just as true if he had been an atheist, because the orbits do not depend on the astronomer's creed. To refuse the truth of a discovery because the discoverer denies God is to punish the gold for having been mined in Egypt.

This does not mean every scientific claim is settled or every theory is sound. Science corrects itself constantly; that self-correction is part of its honesty. And there are places where the prevailing interpretation of the evidence runs past the evidence into philosophy — where a scientist stops describing what is and starts pronouncing on what it all means, which is a different kind of claim requiring a different kind of test. The discipline is to receive the true measurement and to examine the larger claim, to know which is which, and never to confuse the church's authority with a competence it does not have.

I have watched pastors humiliate the gospel by pronouncing on matters of fact they had not studied, as though confidence were a substitute for knowledge. And I have watched the opposite — pastors so eager to be respectable that they handed the whole question of meaning over to the experts, as though a man who can measure a thing must therefore understand what it is for. Both are failures of the same discipline. The first will not learn. The second will not test.

The Proverbs tell us that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge (Proverbs 1:7). The beginning. Not the end. Knowledge has a long road to travel after its beginning, and much of that road runs through laboratories and libraries and the patient work of people who may not fear the Lord at all but who are, without knowing it, tracing the contours of his world.

So here is the posture I am asking for. Listen like a Berean. Receive what is true with gratitude, name its true Owner, and let it correct you where you were wrong. Refuse what is false, and test it by the word and not by your wounded pride. Do not be the Christian who cannot learn because the teacher is an unbeliever. Do not be the Christian who cannot discern because the teacher is impressive.

Both of those Christians have stopped trusting God. One has stopped trusting that his truth can survive contact with the world. The other has stopped trusting that his word is enough to judge the world.

The truth was his before it was ours. We do not own it. We only owe him for it.
chapters.verdict: Truth has only one owner, and he does not lose his title when a skeptic speaks it.
reflect: What true thing have you resisted because of who said it?
How do you tell the difference between testing an idea by Scripture and testing it by your tribe?
Who outside the faith has taught you something true that you have been too proud to credit?

chapters.title: The Honest Unbeliever
chapters.summary: The skeptic who refuses cheap answers is often closer to God than the believer who never had to fight for anything — and the pastor who came in from the outside knows this from the inside.
chapters.body:
There is a kind of unbeliever the church does not know what to do with. Not the mocker, not the man who has never thought about it, not the one who left because the music was bad. I mean the one who actually wrestled. The one who read the arguments, weighed the evidence, looked hard at suffering and hypocrisy and the silence of God, and came away unable to believe — and who is not happy about it. The honest unbeliever. The one whose unbelief costs him something.

I was that person, more or less. So I will not pretend to describe him from a safe distance.

The church's instinct toward such a person is to win, and winning usually means producing an answer fast enough to close the conversation. We have a tract for every doubt, a syllogism for every objection, a one-liner that makes the hard question disappear. And the honest unbeliever sees exactly what we are doing. He sees that we are more afraid of the question than he is. He sees that our certainty is brittle, that it cannot survive being looked at too closely, and the brittleness tells him everything. If your faith cannot bear an honest question, why would he trade his honest doubt for it?

This is where I have to say something the comfortable will resist. The honest doubter is often nearer to the kingdom than the man in the third pew who has never once been troubled by anything. Jesus reserved his hardest words not for the doubters and not for the sinners but for the religious men who were certain — certain of their righteousness, certain of their reading, certain of their place. He told them tax collectors and prostitutes were entering the kingdom ahead of them (Matthew 21:31). The people most sure they were inside were the furthest out. The people who knew they were lost were the ones being found.

There is a man in the gospels who says the truest prayer in the Bible. His son is convulsing, dying, and Jesus tells him everything is possible for the one who believes. And the father cries out, "I believe; help my unbelief!" (Mark 9:24). That is not the prayer of a settled man. It is the prayer of someone holding faith and doubt in the same fist, refusing to let go of either, and Jesus does not rebuke him. He heals the boy. The honest admission of unbelief was not an obstacle to the miracle. It was the doorway.

C.S. Lewis, who came to faith out of a long and serious atheism, understood that the road in is rarely the road of someone who never asked. Lewis called himself the most reluctant convert in all of England, dragged in kicking and looking for an escape. He had read the myths, studied the philosophies, taken the objections seriously because he had once held them himself. His faith, when it came, was the faith of a man who had earned the right to it by refusing every cheap version first. That is why his writing still reaches skeptics a century later. He had been one. He never forgot the texture of it.

Common grace is at work in the honest unbeliever, and we miss it because we are looking for the wrong thing. We are looking for belief, and we do not see the grace operating in the very honesty that keeps him from believing too easily. His refusal of platitudes is a moral act. His unwillingness to say he is sure when he is not is a kind of integrity. His anger at suffering is a recognition that the world is not the way it ought to be — and where do you suppose that recognition comes from? You cannot be outraged that the world is broken unless something in you knows it was meant to be whole. The atheist's protest against evil is borrowed light. He is standing in the glow of a moral order he says does not exist, and the glow is God's.

I learned more about God from honest unbelievers than from many sermons. They would not let me lie. They would not accept the answer that sounded good but did not hold. When I finally came to faith, I came to a faith that had been pressure-tested by people who did not believe, and it was stronger for it. The questions did not destroy me. They built the only kind of faith worth having — the kind that has been to the bottom of the hard things and found something there.

So how does a pastor handle the honest unbeliever? Not by winning. By listening long enough to learn what the doubt actually is, because most of the time it is not the doubt he names first. Behind the intellectual objection there is usually a wound — a father who left, a prayer that went unanswered, a church that was cruel. Peter tells us to always be prepared to give a reason for the hope that is in us, but he does not stop there. He says to do it with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). Gentleness and respect. Not a takedown. Not a victory. A reason, offered the way you would offer water to someone dying of thirst, not the way you would swing a weapon.

I have sat across from men whose unbelief I could not argue away, and I stopped trying. I told them the truth: that I did not have an answer that would satisfy them, that some of their questions were better than my answers, and that I believed anyway — not because the questions had all been resolved but because I had met something, Someone, that the questions could not account for. That honesty did more than any argument. Because the honest unbeliever can smell a salesman, and he can also recognize a fellow traveler who is not pretending the road is smooth.

The Lord is near to the brokenhearted (Psalm 34:18). He did not add a clause excluding the brokenhearted who do not yet believe. The man fighting God in the dark, refusing the easy comfort, demanding that the universe make sense — that man may be closer to the God he is fighting than the man who stopped asking long ago and calls his exhaustion peace.

Do not be afraid of his questions. God is not. The doubt that frightens you is sometimes the very place grace is doing its quiet, common work — keeping a soul honest until the day it can bear the truth.

I know. I was kept honest a long time before I was kept at all.
chapters.verdict: Honest doubt is not the enemy of faith. Dishonest certainty is.
reflect: When did you last take an unbeliever's objection seriously enough to be changed by it?
Are you more comfortable with a doubting Christian or a certain hypocrite, and what does your answer reveal?
What question were you afraid to ask before you believed, and have you stopped letting others ask it?

chapters.title: The Myth of the Empty Field
chapters.summary: The fear that drives Christian isolation imagines a world drained of God, where the church is a lifeboat in a dead sea — but the Spirit was never confined to the church, and the field was never empty.
chapters.body:
There is a story the isolationist church tells itself, and it goes like this. The world out there is a wasteland. God has withdrawn from it. The only living water is inside these walls, and our job is to pull as many people as possible into the lifeboat before the whole ship goes down. Everything outside is contamination. Everything inside is preservation. The less we touch the world, the holier we remain.

It is a powerful story because it has a grain of truth in it. The world is fallen. Sin is real. There is contamination, and there are things a Christian must refuse. But the story takes a true thing and builds a false universe out of it, and the false universe is the myth of the empty field — the belief that God is present here and absent there, that the Spirit clocks out at the church door.

Scripture will not let that stand. Where shall I go from your Spirit? Where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend to heaven, you are there; if I make my bed in Sheol, you are there (Psalm 139:7-8). There is no empty field. There is no square of ground where God is not. The Spirit was hovering over the face of the waters before there was a single believer to receive him (Genesis 1:2). He was at work in the world before the church existed and he is at work in the world the church has not reached. To imagine a God who is confined to the gathered congregation is to imagine a much smaller God than the one who fills heaven and earth.

The myth of the empty field produces a particular kind of Christian, and I have been him. He is anxious. He treats every contact with the wider culture as a risk to be managed. He cannot enjoy a film without first scanning it for danger, cannot read a book by an unbeliever without holding it at arm's length, cannot admire the work of a craftsman who does not share his faith without a twinge of guilt. He has confused withdrawal with sanctification. And the deeper problem is not his behavior. It is his theology. He does not actually believe that God is sovereign over the world he is hiding from. If he did, he would not be so afraid.

Charles Taylor, the philosopher, wrote a long account of how the modern West came to feel that the world is disenchanted — emptied of transcendence, a closed system with nothing beyond it. He called it the immanent frame. Here is the irony the isolationist church has never reckoned with. By withdrawing, by ceding the whole territory of public life and culture and learning to "the secular," the church has confirmed the very disenchantment it claims to oppose. It has agreed with the world that God is not out there. It has said, in effect: yes, the field is empty, and we will huddle in the one corner where he still lives. That is not a refutation of secularism. It is a surrender to it wearing the costume of faith.

Kuyper saw the danger and refused it. He did not pull his people out of Dutch society into a holy ghetto. He founded a university. He went into politics. He built newspapers and institutions and a whole vision of Christians engaging every sphere of life — art, science, government, labor — under the lordship of Christ, precisely because he believed there was no sphere where Christ was not already Lord. His doctrine of common grace was the engine of his cultural engagement. Because God's grace was active in the whole world, the Christian could enter the whole world unafraid, neither contaminated by it nor surrendering to it, but working in it as in a field that belonged to his Father.

Jesus did not pray for the empty-field strategy. On the night before he died, he prayed for his disciples, and he was specific: "I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one" (John 17:15). Not out of the world. In it, kept. He sent them the way he had been sent — into the world, not away from it (John 17:18). The model is incarnation, not evacuation. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14); he did not stay safely in heaven and shout instructions from a distance. He moved into the neighborhood. He ate with the wrong people. He touched the unclean and was not made unclean — he made them clean. That is the direction holiness runs in the gospel. It is contagious outward, not fragile inward.

I want to be careful, because there is a real and ancient calling to be separate, to be holy, to refuse conformity to the patterns of the age (Romans 12:2). I am not arguing that the church should dissolve into the culture until it is indistinguishable from it — that is the opposite error, and it is the subject of the next chapter. I am arguing against a specific lie: that the way to be holy is to believe the field is empty. It is not. And believing it is empty makes us less holy, not more, because it makes us forget that the whole earth is full of his glory (Isaiah 6:3), including the parts of it we have been too frightened to enter.

The cost of the myth is not only to the church. It is to the world that needed us to show up and instead watched us flee. Every sphere we abandoned — the arts, the academy, the public square — did not become neutral when we left. It was formed by whoever stayed. We complain that the culture has gone godless, and we will not admit that we evacuated the building and then blamed the people who moved in. We did this. I did this. We called our retreat faithfulness and then mourned the territory we gave away.

The field was never empty. God was always there, ahead of us, doing the patient work of common grace — restraining evil, sustaining beauty, keeping the human conscience from going entirely dark, planting in unbelievers the very hungers that would one day bring some of them home.

We do not carry God into the world. We follow him into a world where he already is.

The walls we built to keep him pure only kept us from finding him out there. And he was out there the whole time, waiting to be recognized by the people who claimed to know him best.
chapters.verdict: The walls we build to keep the world out also keep our God too small to be worth believing.
reflect: What cultural territory have you abandoned to "the world" that was always God's?
Is your separation from the world about holiness or about fear, and how would you know?
What would your ministry look like if you believed the Spirit was already at work where you have not yet gone?

chapters.title: The Other Cliff
chapters.summary: If isolation is one cliff, assimilation is the other — the church that listens to the world so uncritically that it loses the one thing the world actually needs from it. Common grace requires discernment, not dissolution.
chapters.body:
I have spent four chapters arguing against the church that hides from the world. Now I have to turn and argue against its mirror image, because the doctrine of common grace is balanced on a knife edge, and a fall from either side is fatal. The first cliff is isolation: the church that will not listen. The other cliff is assimilation: the church that listens so completely it forgets it has anything to say.

This is the easier error to fall into right now, and it wears better clothes. It does not look like fear. It looks like humility, like relevance, like finally being reasonable. The assimilated church is tired of being mocked. It is tired of being on the wrong side of every cultural argument. So it begins, quietly, to let the culture set the terms — to decide in advance that whatever the surrounding world has concluded must be where the Spirit is leading, and that the church's job is to catch up gracefully.

It never announces this. It happens by drift. A doctrine that the culture finds embarrassing gets mentioned less, then reinterpreted, then quietly dropped. A moral teaching that the world rejects gets recast as a cultural artifact the church has thankfully outgrown. The cross, which Paul said would always be a stumbling block and folly to the world (1 Corinthians 1:23), gets sanded down until no one could possibly trip over it. And the church congratulates itself on its growth, never noticing that it has talked itself out of the one message it was sent to carry.

Paul saw this coming with terrible clarity. He warned Timothy of a time when people would not endure sound teaching but, having itching ears, would accumulate teachers to suit their own passions (2 Timothy 4:3). Read that carefully. The danger is not teachers the people reject. It is teachers the people choose precisely because those teachers tell them what they already want to hear. The assimilated church does not get conquered from outside. It hires its own conquerors. It selects the voices that will confirm its drift and calls the selection discernment.

Here is the cruelty of it. The world does not actually need a church that agrees with it. It already has the world. It has every institution, every platform, every voice already saying what the world believes. What the world does not have — what only the church can give — is the word from outside, the news that did not originate in the human heart, the announcement that there is a God who made us and judges us and loves us and died for us. When the church surrenders that word in order to be accepted, it removes from the world the only thing it came to deliver. It becomes salt that has lost its taste, and Jesus said exactly what such salt is good for: nothing, except to be thrown out and trampled (Matthew 5:13).

Bonhoeffer watched this happen in real time. In Germany in the 1930s, much of the church assimilated — it adjusted its theology to fit the national mood, blessed what the culture demanded be blessed, and removed the offense that would have cost it its comfort and its safety. Bonhoeffer called the result cheap grace: grace without the cross, forgiveness without repentance, a Christianity that had made peace with the world by ceasing to be Christianity. He paid for his refusal with his life, executed in 1945, weeks before the war ended. He understood that a church which will not be a stumbling block to anything has stopped being the church. It has become a chaplaincy to the prevailing power, blessing whatever the powerful have already decided.

So how does common grace avoid this cliff while avoiding the other one? The answer is in the discipline we have already named: test everything; hold fast what is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21). Hold fast what is good. Not hold fast everything. Not let go of everything. Test, and then keep what passes the test and release what fails it. The same sentence that frees us to listen to the world commands us to judge what we hear. There is no listening without judging. The church that listens and never judges has not embraced common grace. It has abandoned the second half of the verse and kept only the half that costs nothing.

The test is Scripture, and Scripture does not move. That is the whole point of having it. A culture's verdicts shift every generation — what was unthinkable becomes mandatory, what was sacred becomes shameful, and the church that takes its bearings from the culture is taking its bearings from a thing in motion. The word of the Lord stands forever (Isaiah 40:8). The grass withers, the flower fades, the cultural consensus that seemed so permanent dissolves in a generation, but the word stands. A church anchored there can listen to the world without being swept away by it, because it has a fixed point the world does not have.

I have watched both errors destroy ministries. I have watched the isolationist church shrink into a bitter remnant, certain and alone, despised for the wrong reasons. And I have watched the assimilated church grow for a season and then evaporate, because it gave its people the world with a thin religious glaze, and the people eventually realized they could get the world without the glaze and stopped coming. Neither church survived, because both had stopped being the church. One refused to listen. The other refused to judge.

The narrow road runs between them, and it is narrow on purpose (Matthew 7:14). It requires a posture most of us find exhausting: open hands and a firm spine at the same time. Open to learn from anyone, firm to refuse what contradicts the word. Willing to be taught by the world about ten thousand things, unwilling to be taught by the world about the one thing the world cannot know — who God is and what he has done. The discipline is to hold both, and to hold both is to be constantly accused by one side of being the other. The isolationists will call you a compromiser. The assimilationists will call you a fundamentalist. If you are getting both charges, you may be standing in roughly the right place.

I have been called both. On a good day I take it as a sign I have not yet fallen off either cliff.

The world does not need a church that has nothing to say. It is drowning in things to say. It needs the one word it cannot generate from inside itself — and that word is only ours to give as long as we refuse to trade it for acceptance.

Keep the word. Test everything else by it. And do not be surprised when keeping it costs you the very acceptance you were tempted to buy with it.
chapters.verdict: A church that agrees with everything has nothing left to say.
reflect: Where have you adopted the world's assumptions without testing them, mistaking conformity for relevance?
What does your church believe now that it would not have dared believe twenty years ago, and was the change conviction or capitulation?
What truth are you afraid to preach because the culture would punish you for it?

chapters.title: Beauty Was Never Ours Alone
chapters.summary: Art and beauty are gifts of common grace, given to believer and unbeliever alike, and the church that abandoned the arts forfeited one of God's loudest voices to the world.
chapters.body:
Stand in front of a great painting made by someone who did not believe in God, and watch what happens in you. Something rises. A recognition, an ache, a sense that you are in the presence of something true that has nothing to do with the painter's creed. The believer is tempted to feel guilty about this, as though admiring the work of an unbeliever were a small disloyalty. It is not. It is the recognition of a gift, given by God, through a hand that may not have known whose gift it was carrying.

Beauty is common grace in its most undeniable form. The artist who does not pray still makes beauty, because the capacity to make beauty is woven into the image of God in every human being, and that image is not erased by unbelief. It is defaced, the tradition says, but not destroyed. The unbeliever's art is the defaced image still reaching, still making, still bearing witness to a glory it cannot name. Bezalel, the first artist named in Scripture, was filled with the Spirit of God to do every kind of craftsmanship (Exodus 31:3) — and if the Spirit equipped the maker of the tabernacle's beauty, we should not be surprised to find his common grace at work in makers far from the tabernacle.

The church used to know this. For most of its history the church was the great patron of beauty — the cathedral, the oratorio, the illuminated page, the fresco that taught the gospel to people who could not read. The most beautiful objects human beings made for a thousand years were made for worship. Then, somewhere in the last century or so, large parts of the church traded beauty for utility and called it devotion. We built sanctuaries that look like warehouses. We produced art whose only standard was that it carry a message, and a thing made only to carry a message is not art. It is a billboard. We accepted that our art could be mediocre as long as it was sincere, and in doing so we told the watching world that our God inspires nothing worth looking at twice.

That is a lie about God, and the world believed us.

Meanwhile the beauty kept coming — through filmmakers and novelists and songwriters who made no claim to faith and yet could not stop reaching for transcendence. A piece of music written by an agnostic can carry more longing for God than a hundred praise choruses written to a formula, because longing for God is itself a work of common grace, and the formula has none of it. We have all sat in a darkened theater and felt our chest tighten at a story made by people who would deny the very thing the story was straining toward. The straining is the grace. The reaching is the image of God, refusing to stay quiet even in those who say there is no one to reach for.

C.S. Lewis described an experience he called Joy — a sharp, sweet longing provoked by beauty, by a line of poetry or a Norse myth or the smell of a bonfire on an autumn evening — a longing that no earthly thing could satisfy and that pointed, he came to believe, beyond the world entirely. Lewis felt this years before he believed in God. The beauty was working on him while he was still an atheist. It was common grace doing its slow excavation, hollowing out a space that only God could fill, using the pagan myths and the music he loved as the tools. The very beauty he could not account for as a materialist was the thing that would not let his materialism rest.

This is what we forfeit when we abandon beauty to the world. We forfeit one of God's loudest and least defended voices. The skeptic who will slam the door on a sermon will sit for three hours inside a film and let it break his heart, and in the breaking, something gets through that no argument could deliver. The Psalms know this. Their power is not primarily that they teach correct doctrine. It is that they are beautiful — that they say the true thing in a form that lodges in the body and will not leave. He could have given us a theology textbook. He gave us a hymnbook (Psalm 96:1, sing to the LORD a new song). The form was the gift.

I do not mean that all beauty is safe or that the church should swallow whatever the culture calls art. Beauty can lie. It can make the ugly seductive, dress up the false until it goes down easy. Discernment applies here as everywhere; the test of Scripture does not pause when a thing is beautiful. Some of the most dangerous things ever made were beautiful, and their beauty was the bait. So we test. But testing is not the same as refusing, and a church so afraid of beautiful lies that it will not make or receive beautiful truth has surrendered the field to the liars.

The deeper issue is what beauty teaches us about God himself. He did not have to make the world beautiful. Function did not require it. The peacock's tail, the spiral of a galaxy, the particular gold of late afternoon light in October — none of it was necessary for the machinery of the world to run. He made it beautiful because he is beautiful, because out of the overflow of his own glory he made a world that sings. The whole creation is an artwork before it is anything else, and we are made in the image of the Artist, which is why we cannot stop making things even when we have forgotten him. One thing have I asked of the LORD, the Psalmist says, that I may gaze upon the beauty of the LORD all the days of my life (Psalm 27:4). The beauty of the Lord. The deepest human hunger, named as a hunger for beauty — his beauty — and every lesser beauty is a rumor of it.

So receive the rumor wherever it comes from. When an unbeliever makes something beautiful, do not flinch and do not apologize. Say thank you to God, who scattered the gift more widely than we would have, and who is using a thousand makers who do not know his name to keep the human heart from forgetting that it was made for something more.

Beauty was never ours alone. He gave it to the whole world, the way he gives the rain — to the just and the unjust, to the believing and the unbelieving, to the ones who thank him and the ones who never will.

And some of those who never will are, right now, making the very thing that will one day bring a skeptic home. They will never know it. He will.
chapters.verdict: God did not give beauty only to the faithful, and we dishonor him when we will not receive it from the rest.
reflect: When did a work of art made by an unbeliever last move you toward God, and did you let yourself admit it?
Why has so much explicitly Christian art become so bad, and what fear produced it?
What beauty in your city are you walking past every day without thanksgiving?

chapters.title: The Wisdom of the Pagans
chapters.summary: Scripture itself draws on the wisdom of surrounding cultures and commends the prudence of those outside the covenant, modeling the very engagement the isolationist church forbids.
chapters.body:
The book of Proverbs contains material that scholars have long recognized bears a striking resemblance to Egyptian wisdom literature that predates it. The sayings of the wise (Proverbs 22:17 and following) sit close enough to an older Egyptian text that few doubt some relationship between them. Sit with that. The inspired wisdom literature of Israel, the word of God, appears to have engaged, absorbed, and reframed the wisdom of a pagan empire — testing it, correcting it, setting it under the fear of the LORD, and keeping what was good. The Holy Spirit did not consider Egyptian prudence beneath his use. He took the gold of Egypt and carried it into the canon.

If that unsettles you, your doctrine of inspiration is smaller than the Bible's own practice. The wisdom tradition of Israel never pretended that prudence and skill and good judgment were the exclusive property of the covenant people. Wisdom literature is, by its nature, observational. It watches the world — the ant, the sluggard, the harlot, the king, the farmer, the fool — and draws conclusions about how life actually works. And how life works is the same for everyone, because the same God made the world for everyone. The diligent ant teaches the Israelite and the Egyptian alike (Proverbs 6:6). Wisdom is common grace systematized: the accumulated observation of how God's world behaves, available to anyone willing to watch honestly.

Paul stood on Mars Hill in Athens, surrounded by the philosophy of the Greeks, and he did not denounce it wholesale. He quoted it. "In him we live and move and have our being," he told them, and "we are indeed his offspring" (Acts 17:28) — lines drawn from Greek poets, pagan writers, men who worshiped gods Paul knew to be no gods at all. Paul reached into the literature of the people he was evangelizing, found the true thing buried in it, and used their own poets to point them toward the God they were groping after. He did not say their poets were worthless. He said their poets had glimpsed something true and had not followed it home. He took the gold and carried it toward the cross.

This is the model, and the isolationist church has refused the model while claiming to honor the Book that contains it. We have been more suspicious of worldly wisdom than the Bible is. We hear Paul warn against the wisdom of this world (1 Corinthians 1:20) and we conclude that all wisdom outside the church is dangerous, when Paul's point was far more precise. He was attacking a specific thing: the wisdom that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, the cleverness that uses its intelligence to evade the cross, the pride that thinks it has outgrown its need for a savior. That wisdom is folly. But the same Paul quoted pagan poets approvingly in the same career, which means he was not condemning all learning. He was condemning a particular arrogance. The discernment is in knowing the difference, and the isolationist refuses to make the distinction at all, throwing out the prudence of the world along with its pride.

Consider what this costs in the actual practice of ministry. A pastor will counsel a marriage falling apart, and there is a body of careful observation about how human beings damage and heal each other — much of it gathered by people with no faith at all — that is simply true, that describes how God made the human heart to work. The isolationist pastor refuses it because it came from the wrong source, and he counsels with confidence and ignorance, and he does harm. A pastor will lead an organization, and there is wisdom about how groups of fallen people work together or tear each other apart, gathered by observers who never prayed, that is nonetheless accurate about the world God made. To refuse it is not holiness. It is the sluggard's refusal to learn from the ant because the ant is not a member of the covenant.

I have made this mistake. I have stood in front of problems that the wider world had studied carefully and I had not, and I have substituted spiritual confidence for the knowledge I refused to gather, and I have called my ignorance faith. It was not faith. It was pride pretending the fear of the Lord exempts a man from the labor of learning. It does not. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10) — the beginning, the foundation, the right ordering of the whole pursuit — but it is not a substitute for the pursuit. It tells you whose world you are studying. It does not excuse you from studying it.

The test, always, is whether the wisdom submits to the fear of the Lord or sets itself against it. Egyptian prudence about generosity and self-control could be received because it did not contradict the God of Israel; it was reframed under him and kept. The Greek poet's instinct that we are God's offspring could be received because it pointed, however dimly, toward the truth. But the wisdom that exalts the self against God, that promises mastery without submission, that offers a way to flourish without repentance — that wisdom is to be refused no matter how sophisticated, because at its root it is the serpent's old offer to be as gods (Genesis 3:5). The same posture of testing applies. Receive what submits. Refuse what rebels. And know that the difference is not where the wisdom came from but where it is pointed.

There is a particular freedom in this for the pastor. He does not have to pretend the church is the only place anything true has ever been thought. He does not have to choose between honoring Scripture and honoring the genuine insight of the surrounding world, because Scripture itself shows him how to honor both — to learn widely, to test rigorously, to keep what is good, to set it all under the lordship of Christ. He can read the philosopher and the economist and the psychologist the way Paul read the Greek poets: looking for the true thing, ready to use it, never deceived into thinking it is the whole thing.

The pagan who observes the world honestly is reading a book God wrote. He may misattribute it. He may deny the Author on the title page. But the sentences he reads correctly are still God's sentences, and the wise believer receives them with thanks and tests them with care and carries the gold home.

We are not holier than the Book. The Book quotes the pagans. So, when wisdom is wisdom, may we.
chapters.verdict: The Bible quotes the pagans. We are not holier than the book.
reflect: What secular discipline have you dismissed that Scripture might tell you to learn from?
Where do you see God's wisdom operating in people who reject God's name?
Has your fear of "worldly wisdom" kept you from wisdom God meant you to have?

chapters.title: The Restraint We Never Thank Him For
chapters.summary: Common grace includes God's restraint of evil — the reason the world is not as bad as our sin deserves — and gratitude for that restraint reorients how the pastor sees the secular order, including the state and the law.
chapters.body:
We are quick to ask why the world is so bad. It is the wrong question, or at least the second question. The first question, the one almost no one asks, is why the world is not far worse. Given what human beings are, given what is in every one of us, the astonishing thing is not the evil that breaks out but the evil that does not. The restraint is the miracle. And the restraint is common grace.

The Reformed tradition has always taught that one of the great works of common grace is the curbing of sin — that God actively restrains the full expression of human depravity, holding back the chaos that our hearts, left entirely to themselves, would produce. We do not see human nature in its undiluted form because God will not let us. He has placed restraints everywhere: in the conscience, in the family, in the structures of society, in the law, in the state. The world we live in is a world held back from the abyss by the hand of a God who is patient with rebels — including the rebel each of us has been.

Paul makes the most startling claim about this in Romans 13. He says the governing authorities — and he is writing under Rome, under an empire that would eventually execute him — have been instituted by God, that the one in authority is God's servant for our good, that the magistrate who restrains and punishes evil is doing God's work whether he knows it or not (Romans 13:1-4). Read that against the backdrop. Paul is not describing a Christian government. He is describing pagan Rome, and he is calling the Roman magistrate God's servant. The secular order that restrains evil is an instrument of common grace, and the believer who enjoys its protection is enjoying a mercy of God delivered through people who do not acknowledge him.

I do not thank God for this nearly enough, and neither do you. We drive on roads that are mostly safe because most people, most of the time, are restrained from the recklessness their selfishness would otherwise produce. We sleep at night behind doors that are mostly not broken down, in a society where violence is the exception and not the rule, where contracts are mostly honored and the courts mostly function and the lights mostly stay on. None of that is automatic. None of it is owed to us. Every bit of it is a gift held in place by the restraining grace of God working through institutions and consciences and laws made by people who would be offended to be told they were his servants. The settled peace we take for granted is a daily mercy we never name.

This reorients how the pastor sees the world around him. The secular order is not merely the enemy territory the isolationist imagines, nor the savior the assimilationist hopes for. It is, at its best, an instrument of God's common grace — flawed, fallen, capable of becoming a beast that demands worship, and yet, in its ordinary functioning, a gift that holds back the flood. The same Bible that calls the magistrate God's servant in Romans 13 shows the state becoming a monster in Revelation 13, and the pastor must be able to hold both, to thank God for the order the state provides and to resist the state when it overreaches into the worship that belongs to God alone. That is the discernment. But the starting posture, the thing we forget, is gratitude — gratitude for restraint, gratitude that the world is not as bad as we deserve.

Jesus told a parable about a master who let the wheat and the weeds grow together until the harvest, refusing to tear up the field prematurely (Matthew 13:30). There is a patience in God that we mistake for absence. He is not pulling up the weeds yet. He is letting the field grow, restraining the final reckoning, giving time — time for repentance, time for the wheat to mature, time for the honest unbeliever to find his way home. The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, Peter wrote, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9). The delay of judgment is itself a grace. Every day the world continues is a day God has chosen mercy over the reckoning that would end it.

This patience is not weakness, and it is not approval. He restrains evil; he does not bless it. The same God who holds back the flood will one day let the harvest come, and the weeds will be gathered and burned. Common grace is not the same as saving grace, and the restraint of evil is not the forgiveness of it. A man can enjoy a lifetime of common grace — health, prosperity, the order of a stable society, the gifts of intellect and beauty — and still be lost, because common grace was never meant to save. It was meant to sustain, to hold the world open, to give the time in which saving grace could do its deeper work. To mistake the one for the other is to mistake the waiting room for the cure.

But here is what gratitude for restraint does to a pastor. It makes him generous toward the world without being naive about it. He stops seeing the secular order as pure threat, because he recognizes the hand of God holding it together. He prays for kings and all who are in authority (1 Timothy 2:1-2) — not as a grim duty but as a real participation in the work of common grace, asking God to keep restraining the evil that would otherwise consume us, asking God to keep the field open a little longer. And he stops taking the ordinary mercies for granted. The functioning court, the honest official, the law that protects the weak from the strong, the quiet of a city that is not at war — he sees these for what they are: gifts of God, delivered through people who do not know they are delivering them.

I have stood at too many gravesides not to know how thin the order is, how quickly it can tear. And I have come to believe that every ordinary day the tear does not happen is a day God held it shut. The world is not as evil as it could be. That is not an accident of human goodness. There is not enough human goodness to account for it.

It is the restraint of a patient God, keeping the field open, holding back the flood, giving us one more morning we never thanked him for.

We will thank him for it. Or we will discover, too late, how much we were given and never named.
chapters.verdict: The world is not as evil as it could be, and that mercy is God's, not ours.
reflect: When did you last thank God for a secular institution that restrains evil?
How does seeing the state as an instrument of common grace change how you pray for it?
What good order in your life are you enjoying without ever crediting its Giver?

chapters.title: The Image That Would Not Die
chapters.summary: The doctrine of the image of God in every person is the theological root of common grace — the reason the unbeliever can know truth, make beauty, and do good — and the source of the dignity the pastor owes to everyone.
chapters.body:
Everything in this book rests on a single sentence from the first chapter of the Bible. God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him (Genesis 1:27). Pull that sentence out and the whole structure collapses. Common grace, the wisdom of the pagans, the beauty made by unbelievers, the honesty of the doubter, the goodness of the secular order — all of it depends on the fact that every human being still bears the image of the God who made them, and that the image, though defaced by sin, was never erased.

This is the theological root, and we have to get it right, because two errors grow from getting it wrong. The first error says the image was destroyed by the fall — that the unbeliever is so totally corrupt that nothing true, good, or beautiful can come from him, that he is darkness through and through. This is the isolationist's secret theology, and it is false. The fall defaced the image; it did not abolish it. Even after the fall, even after the flood, God grounds the prohibition of murder in the fact that man is still made in his image (Genesis 9:6). After the fall. The image survives the fall. That is why the murder of any human being is an assault on God himself — because the image is still there, in the murderer and the murdered alike.

James says it with a sharpness that should stop every Christian who has ever cursed another human being. With the tongue we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God (James 3:9). Made in the likeness of God — present tense, written to describe people right now, fallen people, people James knew to be sinners. The likeness is current. It did not lapse at Eden. And to curse a person made in God's likeness is to insult the One whose likeness they bear, which is why the casual contempt Christians so often show toward unbelievers, toward enemies, toward the people their politics has taught them to hate, is not a small sin. It is blasphemy by proxy. We did this. I have done this — looked at a person God made in his own image and treated him as an obstacle, a vote, a category, a thing.

The image is why the unbeliever can know truth: because his mind, defaced but not destroyed, is still the mind of a creature made to think God's thoughts after him. It is why the unbeliever can make beauty: because his imagination, fallen but not extinguished, is still the imagination of one made in the image of the Maker. It is why the unbeliever can do genuine good — feed the hungry, love his children, tell the truth at cost to himself, run into the burning building — because the moral capacity God built into the image was not deleted by the fall. The Gentiles who do not have the law, Paul writes, by nature do what the law requires; the work of the law is written on their hearts, their conscience bearing witness (Romans 2:14-15). Written on their hearts. The moral image, still legible, still functioning, still bearing witness even in those who have never heard the law spoken.

Now the second error, which corrects the first by overcorrecting. This error says the image is so intact that the unbeliever needs nothing — that human goodness is sufficient, that the spark of the divine in everyone means everyone is fine, that we are all already God's children in the way that matters. This is the assimilationist's secret theology, and it is just as false. The image survives, but it is defaced, ruined, turned in on itself. The same human being who can make beauty can make a death camp. The same conscience that bears witness can be seared. The image that remains is enough to make the unbeliever capable of truth and goodness; it is not enough to save him, because what is broken in him is precisely his relationship with the God whose image he bears. He can know true things about the world and remain a stranger to its Maker. He can do good to his neighbor and be at war with his God.

The biblical doctrine holds both, and only the biblical doctrine can. The image is real, so we honor every person and expect to find God's gifts in everyone. The image is defaced, so we are not surprised by the depth of human evil and we never mistake common grace for salvation. Hold one without the other and you fall off a cliff. Hold the image without the fall and you become a sentimentalist who cannot account for the camps. Hold the fall without the image and you become a cynic who cannot account for the symphony. The truth is that the same human being is both — capable of more good than the cynic allows and more evil than the sentimentalist will admit, because he is a defaced masterpiece, a ruined cathedral, glory in rubble.

This is the dignity the pastor owes to everyone, and it is not optional. It is not a strategy for evangelism, though it serves evangelism. It is owed to the person because of who made them, regardless of whether they ever respond. The skeptic in your office, the enemy on the other side of every argument, the person whose life and choices appall you — each one is a bearer of the image of God, and you are not free to despise any of them. To despise an image-bearer is to despise the One imaged. There is no human being from whom God's image has been erased. There is no one you have permission to treat as less than that.

Jesus did not look at the woman at the well and see a category — a Samaritan, a woman, a sinner, five husbands and a sixth man who was not her husband (John 4:18). He saw a person, and he asked her for a drink, and he gave her the living water. He looked through the defacement to the image and addressed the image, and the image answered. That is the pastoral art that common grace makes possible: to look at the most ruined person and refuse to stop seeing the cathedral underneath the rubble, to address the image of God in someone who has forgotten they bear it.

The image is why we listen to the world. It is the reason the world has anything to say. The truth, the beauty, the goodness, the wisdom we find out there are all the image of God still speaking through people who have forgotten whose image they are.

It would not die. He would not let it. And the day a pastor truly believes that is the day he can no longer despise anyone.
chapters.verdict: There is no human being from whom God's image has been erased, and no one we are free to despise.
reflect: Whom have you treated as less than an image-bearer, and what did that do to your love?
How does the image of God in your enemy change what you owe him?
Where do you see the defaced but undestroyed image of God in the people your tribe has written off?

chapters.title: When the World Corrects the Church
chapters.summary: Sometimes the world sees what the church has gone blind to, and God uses outsiders to rebuke his own people — a humbling pattern that runs all through Scripture and demands the church listen even to its critics.
chapters.body:
There is a pattern in Scripture that should make every defensive Christian uncomfortable. God rebukes his own people through outsiders. He uses the pagan, the foreigner, the enemy, the one outside the covenant, to tell his people the truth they have refused to hear from their own prophets. It happens too often to be an accident. It is a method.

A pagan king, Abimelech, rebukes Abraham — the father of the faith — for lying about his wife and nearly bringing disaster on an innocent man (Genesis 20:9). The patriarch is in the wrong, and it is the pagan who names it. A Midianite priest, Jethro, watches Moses burning himself out trying to judge all Israel alone and tells him, plainly, that what he is doing is not good, that he will wear himself out, that he needs to share the load (Exodus 18:17-18). The greatest leader in Israel's history receives basic wisdom about leadership from his pagan father-in-law, and Scripture records it without embarrassment, because the wisdom was true and Moses was wise enough to take it.

Jesus did this deliberately, and it enraged the religious. He praised the faith of a Roman centurion above anything he had found in Israel (Matthew 8:10). He made a hated Samaritan the hero of his most famous parable, the one who did the neighborly thing while the priest and the Levite — the religious professionals — walked past on the other side (Luke 10:31-33). He held up outsiders as examples to insiders, again and again, and the message was unmistakable and unwelcome: the people of God do not have a monopoly on doing right, and sometimes the outsider sees and does what the insider has gone blind to.

I want the church to feel the weight of this, because we are very good at deflecting it. When the world criticizes the church, our reflex is to dismiss the criticism on account of its source. They are godless. They hate us. They do not understand. They have an agenda. And sometimes all of that is true and the criticism is still accurate. The fact that a critic is hostile does not make him wrong. Abimelech was a pagan and he was right about Abraham. The world has sometimes seen our sins more clearly than we have, precisely because it was not invested in protecting our reputation, and God has used its clearer sight to rebuke us when we would not rebuke ourselves.

Think of the things the church defended for too long that the watching world condemned first. Think of the abuses the church covered, the hypocrisies it excused, the cruelties it baptized — and how often it was the outside critic, the journalist, the skeptic, the one who owed us nothing, who dragged the thing into the light while the faithful were still circling the wagons. We hate to admit it. We would rather believe that every criticism from outside is persecution. But some of it is prophecy, and the prophet does not have to be a believer to be sent. God spoke through Balaam's donkey (Numbers 22:28). He can certainly speak through a critic who hates us, if we have given him something true to say.

This does not mean every accusation against the church is just. The world does persecute the church, does hate it for the right reasons — for the cross, for the call to repentance, for the refusal to bless what the culture demands be blessed. Jesus promised that hatred (John 15:18-19). So the church cannot simply accept every criticism as gospel; that would be the assimilationist's surrender, taking the world's verdict as final. The discernment, again, is everything. Some of the world's hatred is because we are faithful, and that hatred we wear as a badge. Some of the world's criticism is because we have been faithless, and that criticism we receive as a rebuke from God. Telling the two apart is the hardest and most necessary work, and the temptation is always to file every criticism under persecution so that we never have to repent of anything.

How do you tell them apart? You go back to the word. When the world criticizes the church for failing to live up to the standard of Christ — for greed, for cruelty, for hypocrisy, for protecting the powerful and crushing the weak — the world is usually holding up a mirror that Scripture itself holds up, and the faithful response is to look in the mirror and repent. When the world criticizes the church for holding to the standard of Christ — for calling sin what God calls sin, for refusing to worship the idols of the age — the world is demanding that we stop being the church, and the faithful response is to stand. The first criticism measures us by the gospel and finds us short. The second criticism measures us by the spirit of the age and finds us out of step. The first we receive. The second we refuse. The standard, as always, is the word, not the volume of the complaint.

There is a humility in this that the church desperately needs and rarely has. The willingness to be corrected by an outsider is the willingness to believe that we might be wrong and they might be right, and that God might love us enough to send the truth through a mouth we would never have chosen. Faithful are the wounds of a friend, Proverbs says, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful (Proverbs 27:6) — and yet sometimes the wound comes from an enemy and it is still faithful, still true, still from God. The pride that cannot receive a true word because of who is speaking it is the same pride that crucified the Lord, because his harshest critics were the most religious men of their day, and they could not hear the truth from a carpenter.

I have been rebuked by people who did not share my faith, and the rebukes were just, and I needed them, and my first instinct was always to defend rather than to listen. That instinct is not faithfulness. It is self-protection wearing faithfulness as a mask. The faithful pastor is the one who can hear a hard true word from a critic who owes him nothing, take it back to the word of God, and if the word confirms it, repent — even though the messenger was an enemy, even though it costs his pride, even though the church would rather he had defended its name.

God has never been too proud to rebuke his people through outsiders. We are the ones who are too proud to listen.

And the day the church can no longer hear a true word from outside is the day it has confused its reputation with the truth — and lost both.
chapters.verdict: God has always been willing to rebuke his people through the mouths of outsiders, and we are not exempt.
reflect: When has a critic outside the church told you a hard truth about the church that you needed to hear?
What sin has the watching world seen in the church before the church would admit it?
Are you more loyal to the church's reputation or to the truth, and how do you tell?

chapters.title: The Listening Pastor
chapters.summary: All of it comes down to a posture — the pastor who has learned to listen to the world without surrendering to it, who carries the word as both gift and judgment, and who follows a God already at work ahead of him.
chapters.body:
I started this book as a man who once stood outside the church, certain the interesting people were all out there, and who walked in expecting to be told that everything he had loved was darkness. I want to end it by telling you what I have learned in the years since, because all of the theology in these chapters finally comes down to a posture, and the posture is the whole point.

The pastor who refuses to listen to the world misreads both the world and the Word. He misreads the world because he cannot see the grace already at work in it — the truth in the laboratory, the beauty in the studio, the wisdom in the pagan, the image of God in the enemy, the restraint of evil in the secular order, the honesty in the doubter who will not lie. He looks at a field full of God's working and sees only enemy ground. And he misreads the Word, because the Word itself listens to the world — quotes its poets, absorbs its wisdom, praises the faith of outsiders, receives correction through pagans, and sends its people into the world rather than out of it. The isolationist thinks he is being biblical. He is being the opposite. He is holier than the Book, and that is not holiness. It is a small, frightened theology that has made God smaller than he is.

But I have spent this book equally afraid of the other man, and I will not pretend that danger has passed. The pastor who listens to the world and surrenders to it also misreads both. He misreads the world because he gives it what it already has and withholds the one thing it lacks — the word from outside, the news it cannot generate from inside its own assumptions. And he misreads the Word, because he has taken the half of it that frees him to listen and discarded the half that commands him to judge. He holds fast to nothing. He tests nothing. He has confused the open hand with the empty hand, and an empty hand has nothing to give.

The posture I am asking for is harder than either cliff, and I feel its difficulty every week. Open hands and a firm spine. The willingness to learn from anyone and the refusal to be ruled by anyone but Christ. The capacity to receive a true thing from a skeptic and to refuse a false thing from a friend. The discipline of testing everything by the word and holding fast only what is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21), which means a thousand small judgments a week, each one requiring you to know the word well enough to judge by it and to love the world enough to listen to it first. It is exhausting. It will get you accused from both sides. And it is the only faithful place to stand.

Here is what changes when a pastor finally takes this posture. He stops being afraid. The fear that drove the isolation, the fear that drove the assimilation — both of them are gone, because both of them grew from the same false belief that the outcome depends on him. It does not. The God who sends him into the world is already there. He goes the way the disciples went on the road to Emmaus, walking with people whose eyes were kept from recognizing the Christ who was already beside them (Luke 24:16). His job is not to carry Christ into a Christless field. His job is to help people recognize the One who has been walking beside them the whole time, in their longing for beauty, in their hunger for justice, in their refusal of cheap answers, in the very honesty that keeps them from believing too easily. The grace was already there. He is only late to it.

The harvest belongs to God. Jesus said the fields are white for harvest and the laborers are few (John 4:35), but he never said the laborers grow the wheat. The wheat is already growing. Common grace has been tending the field since before the laborer arrived — restraining the weeds, sending the rain on the just and the unjust, keeping the human heart from going entirely dark, planting the hungers that bring the lost home. The pastor walks into a field God has been working since the foundation of the world, and his task is to bring in what God has grown, to test the harvest, to separate the wheat from the weeds, and to carry the gold of the whole world home to the One who owned it all along.

I think of the people who reached me when I came in from the outside, and I understand now what they were doing, though I do not think they had the words for it. They were not pretending the field was empty. They saw the grace already at work in me — the hunger, the honesty, the ache I could not name — and they helped me see whose grace it was. They did not despise the world I came from. They knew it belonged to God. They listened to me long enough to learn what I was actually asking, and then they pointed me to the One who had been answering before I knew to ask. That is the listening pastor. That is what I have spent the rest of my life trying to become.

So go out. Not out of the world — into it, the way you were sent (John 17:18). Listen to the scientist and the artist and the skeptic and the critic and the enemy, and expect to find God already there, because he is. Test everything you hear by the word that does not move. Hold fast what is good, refuse what is false, and carry the gold home. Honor the image of God in every person you meet, including the ones your tribe has taught you to despise, because there is no human being from whom that image has been erased. And do not be afraid, because the field was always his, the harvest is already growing, and the God who sent you got there first.

I came in from the outside. I know what it is to be a field someone else thought was empty.

It was not empty. He was already there.

He always is.
chapters.verdict: The pastor who will not listen to the world misreads both the world and the Word.
reflect: What in your ministry would change tomorrow if you truly believed God was already at work in the people you have not yet reached?
Where are you still falling off one cliff or the other, and which one is more tempting for you?
Who is the one person God is asking you to stop despising and start listening to?
